items.title: Russian Military-Linked Cargo Ship Burns After Suspected Drone Strike in Gulf of Finland
items.original_title: Russian Military-Linked Cargo Ship Burns After Suspected Drone Strike in Gulf of Finland
items.summary: Flames and thick smoke rise from the Russian-flagged cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on November 21, 2026, following a suspected drone attack. A Russian cargo ship linked to Moscow’s military logistics network caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, drifting into Finnish territorial waters and triggering an emergency maritime rescue operation. The incident took another turn shortly after midday when a Russian helicopter was suspected of entering Finnish airspace near Loviisa, reaching as far as 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory. “The suspected airspace violation may be related to rescue or monitoring operations concerning the damaged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Finland,” Häkkänen said in a statement translated from Finnish. The drone strike prompted Finland to reintroduce temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime activity in the eastern Gulf of Finland. Unlike the Black Sea, where merchant vessels have repeatedly been caught up in military operations, the Gulf of Finland has remained a major commercial shipping corridor despite heightened tensions and security concerns since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The attack on Sparta II raises fresh questions about the vulnerability of Russian military-linked shipping in the Baltic and the potential consequences for neighboring countries when damaged vessels drift across maritime boundaries.

items.summary: The Xeneta Weekly Ocean Container Shipping Market Update provides data and intelligence including the latest freight rate and capacity movements across global trades with supporting insight from Peter Sand, Xeneta Chief Analyst. “Offered capacity is increasing on all fronthauls out of the Far East to Europe and the US, with average spot rates unsurprisingly continuing to soften – with one exception. The trade from the Far East to the Mediterranean is moving in mysterious ways, with spot rates increasing 6.8% in the past week. “Average spot rates into the Mediterranean are now USD 1,551 per FEU higher than into North Europe. “The reason the Mediterranean trade is behaving differently to other fronthauls may be found in the Red Sea, where the ramp-up in services transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait since August tailed off in November. “Something has happened to cool the return of container shipping services to the Red Sea in November. Whatever the reason, disruption in the Red Sea is felt more acutely on trades between the Far East and the Mediterranean because they are the most operationally exposed to the region. “This is a timely reminder to shippers that the path to forecasted falling freight rates in 2027 will not be plain sailing.

items.original_title: Iran War Oil Premium Evaporates as Global Crude Supplies Surge
items.summary: By Nathan Risser and Yongchang Chin (Bloomberg) –The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from. US medium sour export grade Mars traded at a record premium to benchmark West Texas Intermediate futures in the early days of the Iran war. Buyers turned to the Gulf of Mexico variety, which is similar in quality to Middle Eastern crude, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted supplies. On a delivered basis to Northeast Asia, Mars for February was priced at a premium of about $12 to $13 a barrel to the Dubai benchmark — around $10 more expensive than similar quality oil from Saudi Arabia, they said. In Canada, the pipeline that takes oil sands crude from inland fields to export markets on the West Coast is operating at a record 960,000 barrels a day this month, 8% above its stated capacity. Oil will also be shipped on 34 vessels out of the Westridge terminal near Vancouver in November, up from 31 in October. While cheaper heavy crude is a boon to refiners who are already making record profits from the Iran war’s disruptions to global fuel markets, it is coming at a cost to heavy oil producers.

Remedial unit payments go to an IMO fund, and the zero and near-zero reward is paid from that fund by a method not yet written. IMO regimes are usually finished after adoption, and waiting for perfect text means no framework. FuelEU’s review clause requires an evaluation by the end of 2027, and the ETS directive requires a EC report on wider coverage, if there is no global measure by 2028. The useful ask is narrower than adoption or rejection: written fund rules, a reward method and a post-2030 price path, delivered before the vote.

The regulator required the disposal of Seven Borealis to address competition concerns in Brazil’s offshore engineering, procurement, construction, and installation market, where both contractors have a substantial presence. Subsea 7 said the vessel would be sold under an arrangement that allows it to continue fulfilling existing project commitments through a sale-and-leaseback structure. The company has not identified a prospective buyer or disclosed an asking price for the vessel. The planned merger will create Saipem 7, combining two of the world’s largest offshore construction contractors. Subsea 7 said 13 of the 16 relevant competition authorities have approved the transaction. Reviews remain underway in Australia, the EU, and West Africa, with completion now expected in early 2027. The Seven Borealis disposal remains a condition of the Brazilian approval.

items.title: India scraps compulsory retirement age for ships
items.original_title: India scraps compulsory retirement age for ships
items.summary: India has scrapped compulsory retirement ages for ships flying its flag, reversing a policy designed to push older tonnage out of the country’s merchant fleet. The Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) issued a new order this week 18 allowing existing Indian-flagged vessels to continue trading regardless of age, provided they meet prescribed technical and safety standards. The government has also relaxed restrictions on bringing older vessels onto the Indian register. Tankers, bulk carriers and general cargo ships over 20 years old can now be considered for registration, subject to a technical review and approval process. For containerships, gas carriers and chemical tankers, the corresponding threshold is 25 years. The latest move overturns restrictions introduced in 2023 and revised in January this year, which had imposed firm age limits on ships entering and remaining in the Indian fleet. The revised standards also extend to foreign-flagged ships operating in India’s coastal trade under the Coastal Shipping Act 2025. They do not impose a general age restriction on every foreign ship making an international port call in India. The relaxation could help owners seeking to transfer older ships to the Indian flag, including containerline MSC, whose previously announced plan to register about a dozen vessels in India had reportedly encountered difficulties under the earlier age rules.

items.original_title: Greece Has The Most To Lose From Delays In Shipping’s Green Transition, New Analysis Finds

It is separate but related to the risks faced by all shipowners as they manage the energy transition that will also take place within international shipping, whether driven by IMO regulation adopted this December, or postponed global regulation accompanied by a patchwork of regional regulation. The new report finds that the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) is the most credible route to the single global rulebook that the shipping industry, including the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS) has called for. Supporting the NZF, the only adoptable architecture on the table at MEPC 85, is a chance to make the second one, in how shipping’s own energy transition is regulated, predictable, lower burden, less complicated and more supportive of a mix of decarbonisation strategies and pathways.” The report, Real economy consequences for Greece from success or failure of the Net-Zero Framework, is published ahead of ISWG-GHG 23 (23 to 27 November) and MEPC 85, which opens on 30 November.

Under the contract, TMC will supply a complete marine compressed air system, including control and service air compressors, to each of the 23 methanol-ready 87,000 DWT bulk carriers. The marine compressors are based on TMC’s own design, which is developed solely for marine and offshore use. COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry (Dalian) is constructing the vessels for COSCO Shipping Development (Hainan), a wholly-owned subsidiary of COSCO Shipping Development. “These 23 methanol-ready vessels are part of COSCO’s Shipping Development’s response to the green and low-carbon development trend of the shipping industry. This fleet order has therefore been a key target for us and our compressor technologies, which have energy efficiency and reliability at the core. We look forward to contributing towards a large newbuild series of such innovative vessels,” says Hans-Petter Tanum, TMC’s director of sales and business development. According to media reports, the vessels are expected to be delivered between May 2027 and the end of 2028. Source: TMC Compressors

items.title: Smart Sea urges shipowners to tackle ageing infrastructure before investing in new digital solutions
items.original_title: Smart Sea urges shipowners to tackle ageing infrastructure before investing in new digital solutions
items.summary: Shipowners risk undermining their digitalisation efforts by investing in new technology while continuing to operate outdated and potentially vulnerable IT systems, according to maritime technology consultancy SmartSea. Recent fleet assessments by the company have identified vessels still running unsupported operating systems, including Windows 7, raising concerns over cybersecurity, system reliability and the ability to integrate modern digital applications. Kris Vedat, CEO of Smart Sea, warns that too many operators are prioritising new software and connectivity over the infrastructure needed to support them. There’s little point investing in sophisticated technology if the underlying systems aren’t fit for purpose.” Mr Vedat believes the industry needs to move away from short-term technology fixes towards a more co-ordinated approach that includes infrastructure assessments, standardised processes and phased implementation. Technology investments should be judged on the operational value they deliver, not simply the immediate cost savings.” The lack of consistent technical standards across shipping adds to the challenge, particularly for third-party ship managers inheriting vessels with ageing IT and operational technology. Smart Sea believes clearer minimum standards would help improve cybersecurity and support more effective fleet-wide digitalisation. Mr Vedat believes addressing these technical and commercial barriers is essential if shipping is to realise the full potential of digitalisation, automation and decarbonisation technologies.

MARAD’s record of decision approving Texas GulfLink’s application violated the Deepwater Port Act’s requirement that only one deepwater port be approved per application area, the 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals said. Texas GulfLink, to be situated about 30 miles off Freeport, Texas, remains on track for a fourth-quarter 2028 operational date, Bruce Heine, a senior vice president at Sentinel, said this week, adding that given the narrow nature and scope of the issue, there are multiple paths to address the statutory concern without disrupting ongoing construction activities or overall project schedule. items.title: Bayesian Disaster Prompts Calls for Overhaul of Superyacht Safety Standards
items.original_title: Bayesian Disaster Prompts Calls for Overhaul of Superyacht Safety Standards
items.summary: A 3D scan of the recovered wreck of the superyacht Bayesian, which sank off Sicily in August 2024, killing seven people. (Image: UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch) British marine accident investigators are calling for changes to superyacht safety regulations after the sinking of the luxury sailing yacht Bayesian exposed gaps in vessel stability standards, liferaft requirements and crew training that could put other large sailing yachts at risk. The recommendations, contained in the UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch’s (MAIB) final report released Thursday , follow the August 2024 disaster off Sicily that killed seven people, including British technology entrepreneur Mike Lynch and his daughter. Neither the Large Commercial Yacht Code (LY2), under which Bayesian was built, nor the subsequent Red Ensign Group Yacht Code required certain monohull sailing yachts to be assessed for the risk of being knocked onto their sides by high winds when operating without sails. It has also urged the Met Office to raise the treatment of rare but potentially catastrophic weather events with the World Meteorological Organization, while calling for updated guidance in Admiralty nautical publications. “Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised,” said Rob Loder, the UK’s Chief Inspector of Marine Accidents.

items.title: US truckers feel the squeeze as fuel price outpaces freight rates
items.original_title: US truckers feel the squeeze as fuel price outpaces freight rates
items.summary: US shippers using road haulage are increasingly abandoning annual freight contracts in favour of shorter-term agreements, as soaring diesel prices outpace freight rate increases, according to new research from EASE Logistics. The Ohio-based 3PL and 4PL provider’s Q3 26 Automotive Freight Index revealed a sharp shift in procurement strategies, with annual contracts falling from 80% of its automotive bids in September 2025 to just 45% a year later. In food and beverage, the proportion dropped from 81% to 51% by August as shippers sought “greater flexibility amid volatile transport costs”. Diesel prices exceeded $6 a gallon in September for the first time, fuel costs rising considerably faster than freight rates, which EASE reported had increased 27% year on year, compared with a 54% surge in diesel prices. Refrigerated linehaul rates, meanwhile, were up 24% at the end of August, against a 50% increase in fuel costs. Although contract pricing is beginning to catch up, with EASE’s contract cost per mile rising 6.5% between Q2 and Q3, spot rates declined 2% over the same period. Regional disparities are also emerging, particularly in the south-east, where electric vehicle-related freight lanes into Georgia, Tennessee, and Alabama recorded average year-on-year rate growth of 35.6%, compared with 27.4% nationally.

Each vessel will have a capacity of 49,900 dwt, giving the combined order a total of nearly 600,000 dwt. The deal marks the yard’s entry into the MR product tanker segment, adding a new vessel type to a portfolio dominated by LNG bunkering ships, LPG and ammonia carriers, and feeder containerships. Stamford’s involvement first emerged in August, when shipbuilding sources linked the Singapore owner to 10 tankers at the Nantong yard. Stamford has been active in secondhand tankers and bulkers in recent years. The company was previously linked to the acquisition of four ultramaxes from Belships in 2025, while the newbuilding programme would represent a substantial expansion of its tanker interests. For CIMC SOE, the order extends a diversification drive that has already taken the gas carrier specialist into feeder containership construction. The yard has secured orders from owners including Danaos and Euroseas.

items.summary: A strike could disrupt cargo operations at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from Saturday, after the latest contract negotiations between employers and port security workers ended without agreement. The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), which represents shipping lines and terminal operators, warned yesterday that a walkout was a real possibility after talks with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 broke down on Tuesday – each side blaming the other for the lack of progress. Local 26 represents approximately 250 watchmen responsible for security duties, including checking credentials at terminal entrances and conducting patrols. Although they account for only around 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports, a strike could have significant consequences for cargo movements. According to the PMA, approximately 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of LA’s is handled at the terminals where Local 26 members work. Yesterday, the PMA claimed the union had made little progress towards accepting its proposals and was unwilling to extend the current contract beyond 12:01 am on 21 November. Its offer included a one-time $3,200 bonus and wage increases that would bring average annual earnings for full-time watchmen to $198,000, alongside employer-funded healthcare and improved pension benefits.

items.title: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study
items.original_title: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study
items.summary: US corn-based ethanol could offer shipowners a cheaper route to reducing greenhouse gas emissions than low-carbon methanol and ammonia, potentially opening a new marine fuel market for American producers as the global fleet of methanol-capable vessels expands, according to a study released last week. Ethanol could abate about 2.09 metric tons of CO2 equivalent for every $1,000 spent on fuel, compared with 1.30 mt for low-carbon methanol and 1.73 mt for low-carbon ammonia, the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance, an initiative by the nonprofit Global Centre for Green Fuels, said in the study. MEMA estimated ethanol’s well-to-wake greenhouse gas intensity at 34.9 grams of CO2e/megajoule, compared with 15 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon methanol and 10 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon ammonia. In the study, based on classification society ABS’s technical analysis, MEMA assumed US corn ethanol prices on a free-on-board Houston basis at $750/mt, equivalent to $1,125/mt of very low sulfur fuel oil on an energy-adjusted basis. The study’s indicative mid-2026 prices showed ethanol remained substantially more expensive than conventional bunkers but offered lower costs than other low-carbon alternatives. US ethanol supply The US produced 16.4 billion gallons of ethanol in 2025, against an installed capacity of 18.5 billion gallons/year, leaving about 2 billion gallons of spare capacity, according to the study.

items.title: COSCO port fuels growth in APEC trade
items.original_title: COSCO port fuels growth in APEC trade
items.summary: As leaders and delegates focus on advancing regional economic integration under the framework of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a transformative megaproject on the eastern Pacific coast stands as a powerful testament to these shared goals. Chancay Port in Peru, a vital APEC economy, has rapidly evolved into a pivotal logistics hub connecting Latin America with Asia, breathing life into the vision of a seamlessly interconnected Asia-Pacific. Inaugurated in November 2024, the port was hailed by Chinese President Xi Jinping as the starting point of an Inca Trail of the New Era. By slashing the one-way maritime transit time between Peru and China from roughly 35 days to just 23 days, the deep-water port has reduced logistics costs by more than 20 percent, fundamentally reshaping trans-Pacific trade dynamics. Carlos Aquino, director of the Center for Asian Studies at Peru’s National University of San Marcos, said that if Brazil routes its cargo through Chancay to China, it could save upwards of 15 days in transport time, highlighting the port’s immense geopolitical and economic magnitude. Over the past two years, the port has generated $3.65 billion in import and export trade, handling half a million twenty-foot equivalent units of containers. It is projected to bring $4.5 billion in annual economic benefits to Peru and create over 8,000 direct jobs.

items.summary: Norwegian LNG carrier owner ALNG has secured period charters for both its vessels with an unnamed international oil major, taking its entire fleet out of the spot market after a difficult third quarter. The Oslo-listed company, formerly known as Awilco LNG, disclosed that it entered into contracts in October for the 2013-built, 156,000 cu m sisterships WilPride and WilForce . Both vessels have been fixed for worldwide trading, although ALNG said their final charter periods depend on certain conditions. The fixtures follow a period of weak employment for the two-vessel owner. The WilPride completed a six-month charter in early September before moving into the spot market, while the WilForce spent the third quarter trading spot with periods of inactivity. ALNG reported a third-quarter net loss of $5.9m, compared with a $6.4m loss in the preceding quarter. Fleet utilisation improved to 73% from 66%, with average time charter equivalent earnings rising to $38,400 per day from $32,600. Interim chief executive Jens-Julius Nygaard said the new agreements would improve utilisation and reduce the cost of keeping vessels idle during the winter. The move comes after ALNG embarked on a management overhaul earlier this year, including the departure of long-serving chief executive Jon Skule Storheill and a subsequent company rebranding.

items.title: Previous Ukraine port calls could put ships in Black Sea firing line
items.original_title: Previous Ukraine port calls could put ships in Black Sea firing line
items.summary: Merchant ships could be targeted in the Black Sea because of previous visits to Ukrainian ports, even when their current voyages have no connection to Ukraine, according to new intelligence highlighting an expansion of Russia’s maritime targeting campaign, something employed earlier by the Houthis in the Red Sea. British maritime security specialist Ambrey has established that five of the six merchant vessels attacked in Romanian and Bulgarian waters since November 13 had called at Ukrainian ports at least once during 2026. More concerning for shipowners, Ambrey believes there is a realistic possibility that targeting decisions extend beyond individual vessels to include the Ukrainian trading history of other ships operated by the same owner or manager. Ambrey reports that its last confirmed Ukrainian port call was on July 8, more than four months before the attack. The warning comes amid another escalation in attacks on ships, ports and energy infrastructure. Russia’s defence ministry claimed on Wednesday that its drones struck facilities at Ukraine’s Danube port of Izmail and an unidentified cargo ship heading towards Pivdennyi, allegedly carrying dual-use military equipment. Meanwhile, Ukraine confirmed overnight strikes against the Ilsky and Afipsky refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar region, hitting storage tanks and a processing unit respectively. The two facilities have a combined annual crude processing capacity of approximately 13m tonnes.

items.title: Shipping may not return to previous operating environment: CMES
items.original_title: Shipping may not return to previous operating environment: CMES
items.summary: Shipping companies must prepare for lasting changes in trade and security patterns rather than wait for previous operating conditions to return, Wang Yongxin, president of state-controlled China Merchants Energy Shipping, said. Geopolitics, trade relationships, energy systems and supply chains are being reshaped, meaning the industry may not return to its former operating environment even if some risks ease, Wang told the Xinde Marine Forum in Hong Kong. “Many of today’s changes may not be temporary,” he said. “Rather than waiting for that environment to return, companies must make adaptability and continuity of service part of the long-term management.” Wang’s comments followed executives’ warnings during Hong Kong Maritime Week 2026 that a return to past confidence in safe passage might be difficult. “With the way that cheap disposable weapons, if you like, single-use weapons can be deployed across chokepoints at sea, I think it’s very hard for us to see how we can all be as relaxed as we were in the previous 40 years,” Brown said. The tanker fleet had secured employment for about two-thirds of its Q4 operating days and some operating days in 2027, at freight rates substantially above those achieved in January-September. Shipping as critical infrastructure Brown said resilient voyages required cooperation between governments, navies and commercial shipping, alongside efforts to strengthen ships and crews.

items.title: Shipping industry urges governments to agree on global GHG regulations to provide regulatory certainty and incentivize maritime decarbonization
items.original_title: Shipping industry urges governments to agree on global GHG regulations to provide regulatory certainty and incentivize maritime decarbonization
items.summary: The global shipping industry welcomes continuing efforts by all IMO Member States to agree on a global framework of practical, effective and fit for purpose regulations to help decarbonize international shipping and, whilst further improving energy efficiency, continue striving towards the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy goal of net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by or close to 2050. The industry recognizes that all proposals put forward by governments, and the elements these contain, remain under consideration, but emphasizes the importance of an achievable, enforceable, and stable regulatory framework which reflects cost and availability and provides clear incentives for the development and deployment of commercially viable alternative fuels. The regulatory framework must also meaningfully support a safe energy transition through solutions which are data-driven and fuel and technology neutral. The GHG reduction regulations to be adopted by IMO Member States must reward verifiable emission reductions and incentivize, financially and/or technically, further investments that advance maritime decarbonization. In addition, the regulations should also provide optional/flexible compliance mechanisms so that shipping companies, large and small, can manage the transition, recognizing the current unavailability of commercially viable zero/near-zero GHG fuels and technologies (ZNZs) for the majority of the existing fleet. Continued industry investment and effective implementation will depend on global regulatory certainty and the reliable production and cost-competitiveness of alternative fuels at scale.

items.title: Shipping Industry Presses for Global IMO Climate Deal as Divisions Over Rules Persist
items.original_title: Shipping Industry Presses for Global IMO Climate Deal as Divisions Over Rules Persist
items.summary: Nine major shipping associations are urging governments to reach an agreement on global greenhouse gas regulations, warning that continued uncertainty threatens investment in cleaner ships and alternative fuels ahead of critical negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). The joint statement , issued Wednesday, calls for practical, enforceable and globally consistent rules that would give shipowners and fuel suppliers the certainty needed to invest in maritime decarbonization. The appeal comes as governments prepare to revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, whose formal adoption was postponed in October 2025 amid opposition from the United States and several oil-producing countries. The nine organizations—including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERTANKO, INTERCARGO and the World Shipping Council (WSC)—reaffirmed their support for the IMO’s goal of achieving net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. The appeal follows a recent analysis by InfluenceMap that found broad industry support for a global IMO climate agreement, but significant differences over carbon pricing, fuel standards and how emissions from alternative fuels should be calculated. Another point of contention is the relationship between global IMO rules and existing European regulations. The renewed industry push comes ahead of an IMO working group meeting November 23–27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s MEPC 85 session from November 30 to December 3.

items.title: Geneva Dry: TCC’s Emily Koo on the disconnect between dry bulk rates and asset prices
items.original_title: Geneva Dry: TCC’s Emily Koo on the disconnect between dry bulk rates and asset prices
items.summary: TCC Group’s Emily Koo warns that elevated vessel prices, an overreliance on market statistics and a narrow focus on technology risk distracting dry bulk shipping from the bigger challenges ahead. The growing disconnect between freight rates and vessel prices, and the industry’s tendency to overlook what might go wrong, will be among the key talking points when dry bulk executives gather in Geneva next April, reckons Emily Koo of Hong Kong shipowner TCC Group. Koo, one of more than 50 shipowners to take the stage at Geneva Dry 2027, is concerned that the industry is becoming too focused on explaining freight market rallies through statistics rather than examining the underlying health of the shipping business. She questions how long owners can continue justifying the disconnect between earnings and asset values while “sweeping what might go wrong” under the rug. Koo is group managing director and fourth-generation custodian of Hong Kong’s TCC Group, whose origins date to 1917, when her great-grandfather Koo Chung-shui established the family shipping business in Shanghai. The group subsequently relocated its operations to Hong Kong, building a century-long reputation in dry bulk and tanker shipping. Rather than presentations dominated by familiar market data, she wants to hear how industry leaders interpret the challenges facing dry bulk shipping and how they intend to respond.

items.original_title: TARA GAS Burning Off Oman as Another Tanker Attack Leaves 11 Injured
items.summary: A massive fire engulfs what has been identified as the LPG tanker TARA GAS in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters independently verified footage of the burning vessel, although the exact filming date could not be established. (Screenshot from video) The LPG tanker TARA GAS remained on fire and adrift in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, according to a new navigational warning, as independently verified video showed the vessel engulfed in a massive blaze following repeated attacks that left one seafarer missing. The latest developments come as ADNOC Logistics & Services confirmed a separate attack on one of its tankers in the waterway, leaving another crew member missing and 11 injured. A NAVAREA IX navigational warning issued at 1500 UTC Wednesday identified TARA GAS as still burning and drifting southeast, approximately 5.7 nautical miles off Khawr Ghub Ali, Oman. A subsequent attack on November 17 sparked another fire and forced the crew to abandon ship. However, maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified it as the Liberian-flagged product tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which is commercially managed by ADNOC L&S. The reported attack on NAVIG8 MESSI would be the second against the vessel in recent months.

The US naval blockade on Iran-related oil exports was first imposed on April 13 and lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran. “Any ship that receives cargo via a ship-to-ship transfer with a vessel subject to the blockade and carrying cargo loaded at an Iranian port or coastline may be considered to be evading the blockade, even if it has not entered Iranian ports or the Iranian coastline,” CENTCOM said in an update.

items.summary: MSC’s East Mediterranean transhipment hub, in the Turkish port of Tekirdag, is set to almost triple the handling capacity at its Asyaport facility. There are plans to expand the Asyaport terminal, which is 75% owned by MSC, and 25% by the local Soyuer Group, and increase capacity from the current 2.75m teu to 4m teu by the end of the year. The terminal’s deepsea berths are being extended from 1km to 1.4km, while an adjacent feeder pier has already been extended, to 710 metres. The fresh capacity is needed by both port and carrier – according to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, Asyaport handled 2.2m teu last year, representing an annual utilisation rate of 78%, pushing the facility into territory where outbreaks of congestion can be difficult to clear. Throughput this year hit 1.86m teu in the first 10 months, which analysts at Alphaliner suggested “the port is on course to exceed last year’s record”. items.title: Offen firms up four-ship boxship comeback in China
items.original_title: Offen firms up four-ship boxship comeback in China
items.summary: German tonnage provider Claus-Peter Offen has reportedly firmed up all four of its planned 7,000 teu containership newbuildings, ending a nearly two-decade absence from the ordering market. Shipbuilding sources say the Hamburg-based owner has committed to the full quartet after initially signing a letter of intent in September for two firm vessels and two options. China’s Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI), part of state-owned CSSC, remains linked to the deal, although the builder has yet to be formally confirmed. The conventionally powered ships would add around 28,000 teu to Offen’s fleet and mark its first containership orders since 2007. One of the designs gaining traction is SDARI’s compact Sealion 7100, which measures 255 m in length and 42.8 m in breadth, with capacity for up to 1,143 reefer containers. For comparison, South Korea’s Namsung Shipping has recently been linked to two firm 7,100 teu ships plus two options at China’s Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Corporation, with brokers putting the price at around $89m per vessel. Its last containership newbuilding programme dates back to before the 2008 financial crisis, with the final vessels arriving several years later after construction delays. Among the youngest ships stemming from that earlier investment are the 2012-built, 5,574 teu MSC Coruna and MSC Vigo, both still listed in the company’s fleet under MSC employment.

items.title: European Natural Gas Prices Hold Gains
items.original_title: European Natural Gas Prices Hold Gains
items.summary: European natural gas prices held their recent advance above €85/MWh on Wednesday, as traders weighed persistent tensions in the Middle East and Europe’s winter supply outlook. Renewed fighting and a series of vessel strikes around the Strait of Hormuz have heightened concerns over sustained disruptions to LNG shipments from the Persian Gulf. The gas market remains tight amid curtailed Qatari supplies and the bloc’s depleted gas inventories. European gas reserves fell toward 70%, compared with the five-year seasonal average of 89%, leaving the region more exposed to price spikes when severe cold spells set in. Colder weather is forecast across much of Europe, potentially boosting heating demand and accelerating storage withdrawals. Meteorologists also see an increasing likelihood that the earliest-ever recorded breakdown of the polar vortex could send a blast of cold Arctic air southward from the Nordics in late November or early December. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
items.original_title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
items.summary: Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions. The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) later this month, with governments still divided over how to regulate and price shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions. BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), Intercargo, Intertanko, the World Shipping Council, Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), Interferry, the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) and the International Parcel Tankers Association (IPTA) have called for a single global framework that applies equally to vessels regardless of flag, ownership or trade. The groups warned that national and regional schemes could result in duplicated compliance requirements and multiple charges for the same emissions, undermining efforts to establish a level playing field. The intervention comes after the IMO failed to secure agreement on its proposed Net-Zero Framework in October 2025, forcing governments to postpone adoption for a year. The industry’s latest appeal follows growing concern over the spread of regional carbon schemes. Several African governments are moving towards their own shipping emissions charges, while European operators already face the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations.

items.title: How Global VE Trading Cut Routine Vessel Screening from 30 Minutes to Five
items.original_title: How Global VE Trading Cut Routine Vessel Screening from 30 Minutes to Five
items.summary: Global VE Trading is a Malaysia-based floating storage and ship-to-ship (STS) service provider, serving some of the world’s largest oil companies and commodity traders. Operating in a highly regulated industry, Global VE Trading must meet its customers’ stringent compliance standards while protecting its own business from sanctions exposure. Reliable vessel screening is essential to maintaining customer trust, safeguarding insurance coverage, and keeping business moving. A Small Team, High Volumes, and Manual Checks Global VE Trading is responsible for screening every vessel entering its Malaysian anchorages, and with 300-1,000 screenings handled by two analysts every month, efficiency is critical. Global VE Trading needed greater visibility into behavioral risks, but equally important was the ability to distinguish genuinely suspicious activity from legitimate technical or operational issues. With Windward’s Risk & Compliance solution, Global VE Trading has significantly reduced the time spent on routine vessel screening while gaining a more complete view of each vessel’s risk exposure. Low-risk vessels that previously took at least 30 minutes to screen can now be cleared in approximately five minutes. Straightforward vessel screenings now take approximately five minutes, compared with at least 30 minutes previously. Looking Ahead As maritime sanctions risks evolve, Global VE Trading is looking to build on its efficiency gains with an even more proactive approach to compliance.

items.title: Global spot gas prices skyrocket but European buyers should stick to spot-indexation, experts say
items.original_title: Global spot gas prices skyrocket but European buyers should stick to spot-indexation, experts say
items.summary: Europe’s share of LNG imports bought on a spot basis was 36% in 2026 year to date. This compared to 38% in full year 2025 and 35% in full year 2024 according to ICIS data. This means that although oil prices have risen, major LNG buyers in Asia that take most of their LNG on long-term contracts indexed to oil have likely not seen their overall weighted average cost of gas imports rise as much as those in Europe buying almost entirely at spot gas market related prices. The massive increase in European and global spot prices and Europe’s increasing exposure to them has raised two questions: does Europe need to change its purchasing strategy and sign more long-term deals and will that also reopen the debate of oil versus spot indexation in such sale and purchase agreements? During times of more plentiful supply this served Europe well, with spot gas prices looking competitive against oil for the decade from 2010 to 2020. So, should European buyers be looking again at how to index their deals and the comparison between oil and spot gas? Market experts polled by ICIS said the current market dynamics and extremely high spot gas prices are not likely to lead to a new shift towards oil-indexation in long-term deals.

items.title: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
items.original_title: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
items.summary: India’s push to expand domestic shipbuilding and lessen its dependence on China has found an eager partner in Korea, whose shipbuilders are looking for new production bases abroad. Those complementary needs are driving a burgeoning partnership centered on Thoothukudi, a port city near India’s southern tip, where HD Hyundai plans to build a $4 billion shipyard with Indian state partners. On India’s west coast, Samsung Heavy Industries is backing an Indian yard competing for the country’s first oil tanker orders in decades. When India’s shipping minister visited Korea last month, he toured Korean shipyards and explored business opportunities with all three of Korea’s major shipbuilders, underscoring New Delhi’s push to expand its shipbuilding industry. About 95 percent of India’s trade by volume moves by sea, the country spends close to $75 billion a year hiring foreign ships, and its own yards held 0.5 percent of the global order book as of Sept. Chinese yards won 63 percent of global new orders last year and Korean yards 21 percent, according to Clarksons Research. “After Southeast Asia, India is the market drawing attention,” the representative said, adding that India is courting Korea’s three major shipbuilders to grow its own industry.

items.title: Global crude surplus will reach 2 million b/d in 2027: Goldman Sachs
items.original_title: Global crude surplus will reach 2 million b/d in 2027: Goldman Sachs
items.summary: The global oil market is heading for a 2 million barrels/day surplus in 2027 as Persian Gulf liquids output is expected to rise by nearly 4 million b/d above current levels and new pipeline infrastructure will route an increasing share of Gulf supply around the Strait of Hormuz, Goldman Sachs analysts said. The investment bank’s base case projections are underpinned by a sharp recovery already underway in Gulf crude exports, with Goldman Sachs estimating that Gulf crude exports rose 2 million b/d month over month in October, recovering to their 2025 average. That rebound drove a major reversal in global liquids balances, shifting the market from a 600,000 b/d deficit in September to a 1.6 million b/d surplus in October, according to the bank. Goldman Sachs forecasts an additional 3.8 million b/d of pipeline bypass capacity to come online over the next year. By end-2027, this infrastructure build-out should allow Gulf countries to export over 14 million b/d — or around 60% of their 2025 average export volumes — via pipelines bypassing Hormuz alone, Goldman Sachs said. Goldman Sachs said this would help global stocks recover from current low levels, with the 2027 supply-demand surplus, measured as oil production minus oil end-use demand, reaching 2 million b/d.

items.title: UK sets out 2030 marine fuel crackdown
items.original_title: UK sets out 2030 marine fuel crackdown
items.summary: Britain has laid out plans for a new shipping fuel regulation that could initially cover around 5,000 vessels calling at its ports, including ships operating on international routes. The Department for Transport opened a consultation this week on a proposed greenhouse gas intensity standard, which the government expects to introduce from 2030. The regime would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gt and above, irrespective of flag, requiring operators to progressively reduce the lifecycle emissions intensity of the fuels and energy they use. Britain is taking its lead from the EU’s FuelEU Maritime framework, which entered into force in January 2025, while seeking to retain flexibility around future IMO requirements. Government modelling suggests 4,913 vessels of at least 5,000 gt called at UK ports in 2019. Another 2,405 smaller ships could eventually be brought into the regime if the threshold is lowered to 400 gt. The latest move comes after domestic shipping was brought into the UK Emissions Trading Scheme in July. British shipowners have already warned against copying the administrative problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime. In October, the UK Chamber of Shipping called for better-aligned reporting systems and realistic targets reflecting the availability of alternative fuels.

items.title: Smaller Tankers Join Hormuz Shuttle Trade to Keep Oil Flowing
items.original_title: Smaller Tankers Join Hormuz Shuttle Trade to Keep Oil Flowing
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Oil/Chemical Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo Nov 18, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Oil is increasingly moving through the Strait of Hormuz on smaller vessels, helping sustain exports as attacks on supertankers squeeze availability of the ships that typically dominate the trade. The volume shipped through the waterway by Suezmaxes and Aframaxes has climbed over the past two months, hitting a wartime high of more than 2 million barrels a day in October, according to Vortexa. The lucrative but risky trade of shuttling crude out of the Persian Gulf during the US-Iran war has primarily relied on very large crude carriers, which can carry up to 2 million barrels. The supertankers account for 72% of the vessels transiting Hormuz, according to BRS Shipbrokers, although they have become the target of Iranian attacks, taking some out of operation. The tankers either transfer crude to other ships after passing through Hormuz or sail directly to ports, often in India. The vessel previously transported crude from Russia’s western ports to India, a trade permitted as long as the oil complies with price-cap guidelines imposed by the Group of Seven nations.

items.summary: BW Group-backed Hafnia has abandoned its pursuit of Danish product tanker rival Torm and is preparing to unwind its near-20% holding after failing to win support for a combination of the two shipping giants. The Oslo- and New York-listed owner said on Wednesday it intends to exit its entire 19.85% stake, preferably by distributing its 20.36m Torm shares to Hafnia shareholders through a special dividend. The holding was valued at $686.6m based on Torm’s November 17 closing share price of $33.73.The move brings an abrupt end to a consolidation push that saw Hafnia spend more than $500m building its position in Torm over the past year. Under the proposed exit, Hafnia shareholders would receive one Torm share for every 26.3 Hafnia shares held, with fractional entitlements settled in cash. The distribution, worth approximately $1.28 per Hafnia share at Tuesday’s closing price, would replace the company’s regular cash dividends for the third and fourth quarters. Hafnia said it needs cooperation from third parties to complete the transaction and has set November 25 as the deadline. Hafnia began building its position in September 2025 when it struck a deal with Oaktree Capital Management to acquire around 14.16m Torm shares for $311.4m, at $22 apiece. Those purchases took its holding to 19.85% and made Hafnia Torm’s largest disclosed shareholder.

items.title: Dry bulk FFA trading heads for another record year
items.original_title: Dry bulk FFA trading heads for another record year
items.summary: Trading in dry bulk forward freight agreements (FFAs) is heading for another record year, with volumes already approaching last year’s total as geopolitical upheaval drives greater demand for freight hedging. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers, using Baltic Exchange data, shows that 3.16m FFA lots changed hands between January and October, up 12% year-on-year and just shy of the 3.33m lots traded throughout 2025. The market has more than doubled in size since 2020, when annual turnover stood at 1.56m lots. Supramax contracts have recorded the fastest growth this year, with trading jumping 28.1% to 578,772 lots. Activity has subsequently moderated, although October’s 325,531 lots remained 17.4% above the corresponding month last year. The expanding market was a major talking point at this year’s Geneva Dry conference . “Liquidity in the market can only be good for it,” Karen Taylor, head of industrial commodities at ADM Investor Services, told delegates, highlighting how much easier it has become to trade FFAs compared with a decade ago. FFAs will form part of the discussion in the Risk Management In Dry Bulk panel at the 2027 edition of Geneva Dry on April 27. ICAP launched a dedicated global dry FFA desk in April, linking trading hubs in London, Copenhagen, Dubai and Singapore.

items.title: Fresh tanker attack in Hormuz highlights ongoing threats facing Gulf shipping
items.original_title: Fresh tanker attack in Hormuz highlights ongoing threats facing Gulf shipping
items.summary: A new tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz has been reported by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre, in the latest of a string of incidents targeting vessels attempting to traverse the vital waterway. In a statement dated Monday, the British trade monitor said a third-party had reported that the attack had disabled the ship and sparked a fire in the engine room. The crew are reportedly safe, while the damage assessment and environmental impact of the attack was unknown. The UKMTO reiterated a recent warning that vessels should transit Hormuz with “caution.” Since November 10, the UKMTO has reported seven attacks in or near Hormuz, a key conduit for roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the outbreak of the Iran war in late February. Despite moves by Iran to stem traffic through Hormuz, shipping data have indicated that more tankers are making the sailing thanks in part to increase U.S. security in the region. Still, the attacks have sustained fears of possible disruptions to oil flows out of the Gulf region, while messaging around negotiations to end the Middle East conflict has been muddled.

items.title: Fuel Switch Snapshot: LSMGO undercuts LNG and LBM for diesel SS engines
items.original_title: Fuel Switch Snapshot: LSMGO undercuts LNG and LBM for diesel SS engines
items.summary: A $102/mt drop in Rotterdam’s LSMGO over the past week has made the conventional fuel grade cheaper than both LNG and liquefied biomethane (LBM) in the port for vessels with diesel slow speed (diesel SS) engines. LNG prices have dipped $8-9/mt and LBM prices have fallen $13-14/mt depending on engine type in the same period. LNG burnt in diesel SS engines has flipped from a $78/mt discount to LSMGO to a $15/mt premium over the past week. LNG’s premium over LSMGO has widened by $94/mt to $122/mt for Otto MS engines, and LBM’s by $89/mt to $174/mt. For vessels with diesel SS engines, it has narrowed by $5/mt to $47/mt. Singapore’s LNG prices have fallen by $131/mt for both engine types, as the JKM contract they are priced on has moved from December to January delivery, a move that accounts for $75/mt of the fall and leaves both down by $56/mt without it. For vessels with Otto MS engines, LNG’s premium over LSMGO in Singapore has narrowed by $136/mt to $141/mt. For vessels with diesel SS engines, it has narrowed by $136/mt to $88/mt. LNG’s premium over B100 for vessels with diesel SS engines has narrowed by $117/mt to just $3/mt over the past week.

items.title: How to Reduce False Positives in Vessel Screening Without Missing Real Risk
items.original_title: How to Reduce False Positives in Vessel Screening Without Missing Real Risk
items.summary: Screening Alerts Are a Volume Problem Before They Are Anything Else Every compliance team that touches maritime trade runs vessels through a screening system before a transaction proceeds. The system checks the vessel against sanctions lists, looks at its recent movements, flags anything that resembles a risk indicator, and produces an alert. An alert is a referral, not a finding. A screening system producing false positives at scale cannot reliably distinguish a vessel that looks like a risk from a vessel that is one. Not only what the AIS record shows, but what the vessel has done over time, who owns it through how many layers, how its behavior compares to vessels confirmed as illicit, and whether the data source that triggered the alert is even reliable in the environment where the event occurred. The Noise Has Specific Causes False positives in vessel screening are not randomly distributed across the fleet. Windward recorded dark convoy passages accounting for 47% of Strait of Hormuz transits in August 2026 and 52% in September, as vessels crossed with AIS off for crew and vessel safety. Each comes from what the screening system is reading, or failing to read, which means each has an answer in the data rather than in the sensitivity setting.

items.title: How the Hormuz crisis handed America a lasting export advantage
items.original_title: How the Hormuz crisis handed America a lasting export advantage
items.summary: As Middle Eastern supplies faltered, American exporters of LNG, LPG, jet fuel and plastics gained new customers, new shipping routes and, in some cases, contracts stretching decades into the future. Alex Byelyavtsev reports. When the Strait of Hormuz became unreliable in 2026, some of the world’s largest suppliers of energy and industrial materials lost their normal access to customers overseas. Enterprise Products Partners was already expanding propane and butane export capacity at its Houston Ship Channel terminal by another 300,000 barrels a day, illustrating how established American terminals were positioned to handle greater demand. A buyer who previously received propane from the Persian Gulf might now need a gas carrier to collect it in Texas. According to US government energy data, jet-fuel exports averaged 356,000 barrels a day in the second quarter of 2026, more than double the five-year average. Plastics and resins accounted for about 45% of Port Houston’s containerised export teu in 2025. Across the United States, exporters booked more than 6,000 containers of plastic materials in a single day in March, well above normal levels. Its contract is secure, the cargo is available, and a ship can be arranged.

items.title: Gulf Oil Flow at Risk From Lack of Empty Tankers, Tracker Says
items.original_title: Gulf Oil Flow at Risk From Lack of Empty Tankers, Tracker Says
items.summary: By Alaric Nightingale (Bloomberg) — The number of empty tankers sailing to collect cargoes of Middle East crude is sliding, a trend that could jeopardize the recent revival in the region’s oil flows to global markets, according to Tankertrackers.com, a firm that monitors vessel movements. The industry uses two main ship types to get oil from the Persian Gulf to the world: very large crude carriers, which transport 2 million-barrel cargoes, and Suezmaxes that move about half that. The collective capacity of those vessels sailing empty to the region has declined by about 40% since the end of August, according to Tankertrackers.com figures. The Iran war has meant that some vessels refuse to go through the Strait of Hormuz, instead receiving cargoes in locations like the Gulf of Oman from tankers that are willing to risk shuttling through the crucial waterway.

items.title: StealthGas crew airlifted from stricken LPG carrier off Bulgaria
items.original_title: StealthGas crew airlifted from stricken LPG carrier off Bulgaria
items.summary: All 19 crewmembers of a StealthGas LPG carrier have been rescued after the vessel was caught up in a suspected drone attack off Bulgaria, the second serious merchant shipping incident in the western Black Sea in less than 24 hours. The Liberia-flagged, 7,500 cu m Gas Husky got into trouble overnight on Monday while sailing from Alexandria, Egypt, towards Romania’s Midia port. The 2012-built vessel disappeared from tracking systems shortly after midnight, with its emergency position-indicating radio beacon activated around 8 am local time on Tuesday. The 7,218 dwt fully pressurised LPG carrier forms part of Harry Vafias-led StealthGas’s fleet. The ship was approximately 14.5 nautical miles from the location where the Somali-flagged general cargo vessel Betul 8 capsized on Monday. That vessel, carrying around 3,000 tonnes of wheat from Romania to Egypt, was reportedly struck by two unmanned surface vessels before taking on water. All 12 crewmembers were rescued in an operation involving Bulgarian, Romanian and Turkish forces. Maritime security consultancy Diaplous has recorded at least 17 merchant vessels attacked off Romania and Bulgaria since mid-July, with several casualties reported in recent weeks. The latest incidents have occurred close to shipping routes used by vessels trading to and from Ukrainian and Romanian Black Sea ports.

items.original_title: Gemini carriers target complete return to Suez transits by mid-January
items.summary: Gemini Cooperation partners Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd will have made a full resumption of Suez transits on their Asia-Europe services by mid-January. Yesterday, the partners outlined the schedule for the last three Asia-North Europe services still detouring via the Cape of Good Hope to return to the Red Sea routing. The Asia-Northern Europe Loop 1 (Maersk AE2/Hapag-Lloyd NE1) will resume Suez transits in both directions with the departure of the 18,300 teu Mary Maersk from Ningbo on 4 December. The Asia-Northern Europe Loop 3 (Maersk AE3/Hapag-Lloyd NE3) will also fully resume westbound Suez transits following the departure of the 16,300 teu Alette Maersk from Shanghai on 20 December. Meanwhile, shippers on the Asia-Northern Europe Loop 2 (Maersk AE1/Hapag-Lloyd NE2), operated entirely by Hagag-Lloyd vessels, will have to wait until early 2027, with a full westbound resumption beginning with the departure of the 23,700 teu Damietta Express from Shanghai on 14 January, representing the last of Gemini’s Asia-Europe strings to return to Suez. It also remains to be seen how the widespread return to Suez routings will impact Asia-Europe schedule reliability, which according to Xeneta data, has fallen to historic lows – just 4% of vessels arrived on time in Europe ex-Asia in September, which rose to 7% in October.

items.title: Box ship charter rates still climbing as lines hunt for more tonnage
items.original_title: Box ship charter rates still climbing as lines hunt for more tonnage
items.summary: Charter prices for containerships continue to defy the cooldown in long-haul freight rates, as major operators continue to hunt tonnage. Linerlytica this week reported that French line CMA CGM took the 2001-built 5,610 teu Aigio (previously known as Wan Hai 611 ) for 3.5 years. While the rate was not disclosed, charter rates for similar-size vessels are around $66,000 a day, up 10% year on year. Aigio is one of three sister ships Wan Hai sold in March for $34m to $38m each, Greek tonnage provider Costamare buying two and CMA CGM the other – Wan Hai 612 and Wan Hai 613 have not been renamed or delivered yet. Charter rates for box ships of all sizes have risen by between 7% and 23% year on year, with feeder vessels registering the biggest gains due to higher demand from intra-region trades and the lack of newbuilds in recent years. A 1,700 teu ship is now going for around $32,000 a day. “The strong demand in the containership charter market continues, with charter rates still edging upwards, with forward fixtures stretching into the end of 2027,” Linerlytica said. Meanwhile MSC, by far the busiest buyer of second-hand ships, continues to hunt for tonnage to consolidate its lead over its peers.

items.title: More pain for India-Gulf shippers as costly box returns add to rising rates
items.original_title: More pain for India-Gulf shippers as costly box returns add to rising rates
items.summary: Apart from the lingering pressure of ocean freight rates that remain stubbornly elevated, India-Middle East shippers are facing various extra cost shocks, due to shifting carriers’ cargo handling policies and landside supply chain hurdles in the conflict region. According to industry sources, fresh booking curbs imposed by mainline operators like Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have further constrained capacity options for India’s cargo flows to the Persian Gulf. With available vessel space from JNPA (Nhava Sheva) and Mundra to Khor Fakkan and Fujairah in the UAE, and Sohar in Oman, becoming tighter and more erratic, rates for these “lifeline” port pairs have risen from the levels seen last month, data suggests. Spot rates offered by CMA CGM for JNPA to Khor Fakkan are around $7,500 per 40ft, compared with $6,500 to $7,000 in the second half of October. “With fewer sailings, active capacity providers have the room to adjust rates dynamically.” Rates ex-India to the other Gulf ports of discharge have also climbed month on month because of the supply-side issues, sources said. CMA CGM’s spot rates for a 40ft booking from JNPA to Sohar are around $6,500, nearly double what the carrier was quoting at the end of September. And the Gulf trade pain for shippers goes beyond soaring ocean rates.

items.original_title: US set to benefit most as Iran conflict reshapes global LNG trade, says GlobalData
items.summary: It accounts for more than half of internationally traded gas to support diverse energy needs. However, geopolitical tensions have caused supply-side disruptions to LNG trade. The war in Ukraine has been the central shock, accelerating Europe’s structural pivot away from Russian pipeline gas and toward seaborne LNG, which in turn has increased Europe’s reliance on global spot cargoes and reduced supply flexibility for price-sensitive importers.” While Iran is not a large LNG exporter, the conflict has sharply reduced regional output and disrupted shipping continuity.

Under a separate scenario where Gulf LNG exports remain at approximately 35% of pre-war levels through the end of 2027, Goldman Sachs estimates TTF prices would average 104 EUR/MWh in 2027. The projections appear in Exhibit 6 of the firm’s analysis on European Union gas prices. The forecasts link European gas price movements to the level of LNG export recovery from the Persian Gulf region. items.title: African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping
items.original_title: African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping
items.summary: A growing group of African nations is pushing ahead with plans to introduce carbon charges on international shipping, raising the prospect of another regional emissions regime for shipowners already grappling with European environmental legislation. Guinea, Ivory Coast and Mauritania have signed an agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, to develop a coordinated approach to charging ships for their carbon emissions. The initiative, promoted by the Africa Sovereign Carbon Registry Foundation (ASCRF), builds on existing schemes in Djibouti and Gabon, with the ambition of establishing a continent-wide framework for raising climate finance from international shipping and aviation. Under the model pioneered by Djibouti, vessels are charged $17 per tonne of CO2 calculated on 50% of emissions from voyages to and from the country’s ports. The latest agreement brings the number of countries associated with the proposed African coalition to six, although the status of Liberia’s involvement remains contentious. Monrovia stated earlier this year that it would not impose a unilateral carbon levy on international shipping. Other African countries are considering similar schemes. The development comes at a particularly sensitive moment for shipping’s decarbonisation negotiations, with the International Maritime Organization due to resume discussions on its proposed global emissions framework later this month.

items.summary: The European Union has widened its sanctions campaign against Russia’s shadow fleet, targeting tanker owners, shipmanagers, insurers and oil buyers across several countries in a fresh effort to disrupt Moscow’s seaborne energy exports. The measures adopted on Monday add 12 individuals and 101 entities to the EU’s sanctions lists, including companies in the UAE, China, Seychelles and Oman involved in trading Russian oil. Among those targeted are Dubai-based Lidoil DMCC, Spikoil DMCC, Lynx Ship Management, Stalwart Shipmanagement, Grace Shipmanagement and Greenlight Shipmanagement. The crackdown extends to JSC Petersburg Oil Terminal, which operates oil export infrastructure in the St Petersburg region. Nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions have also been sanctioned, tightening restrictions on the financing of the country’s energy trade. The measures impose asset freezes and prohibit EU businesses from providing funds or economic resources to the designated entities. The latest action follows Britain’s blacklisting of 11 additional vessels last week and comes amid intensifying European scrutiny of Russia’s international tanker operations. France and Britain will host an international conference in Paris on December 4 to coordinate further action against the shadow fleet. More than 670 vessels are already subject to EU port access and maritime services restrictions.

items.summary: China’s transformation from the world’s dominant dry bulk importer into an increasingly significant exporter is gathering pace, with outbound cargo volumes more than doubling since 2020 and accounting for nearly two-thirds of global dry bulk shipment growth this year. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers, using Signal Ocean vessel-tracking data, shows Chinese dry bulk loadings reached 274.9m tonnes in the first 10 months of 2026, up 14.9% year-on-year China accounted for 35.6m tonnes of the 54.4m-tonne increase in global dry bulk loadings during the period, an extraordinary contribution from a country traditionally viewed principally as a destination for raw materials. Its share of worldwide dry bulk loadings has climbed from just 2.5% in 2020 to 5.5% this year, with annual export shipments rising from 128.6m tonnes to 291.5m tonnes between 2020 and 2025. “From being an almost sole importer of dry cargoes [China] has emerged into a large exporter over the last few years, a very interesting development indeed,” Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chairman and chief executive of Norwegian owner Belships, told Splash in an interview last week. Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group, puts the succession challenge sharply: “Shipping therefore has to compete for family capital rather than assume it will inherit it.” More importantly, he argues, the next generation must be able to build a modern shipping enterprise in Hong Kong, not simply administer ships acquired by their parents or grandparents. Hong Kong-listed Pacific Basin moved strategic leadership and commercial decision-making to Singapore in 2025 amid US-China port-fee tensions, while Seaspan also relocated its headquarters to the city-state. The threat, therefore, is not an imminent extinction of Hong Kong’s shipping families. If the next generation continues to own vessels but chooses to finance, charter and direct them elsewhere, Hong Kong can retain impressive maritime statistics while losing some of the commercial influence that made those statistics possible.

An example in Terminal Activity Using the Terminal Activity workspace in Container Intelligence, we can take four carrier groups calling San Pedro, Seattle, and Tacoma on vessels above 5,000 TEU, benchmarked against each other from January through September 2026: MSC is the dominant carrier at these ports by volume, with 122 terminal calls across the period, more than the other three carrier groups combined. items.summary: This means the global fleet will remain dependent on fossil fuels, or their bio- or e- equivalents, for years to come and must find novel ways to reduce emissions. Energy-efficiency measures reduce fuel consumption, but even those more efficient crossings will continue to produce carbon emissions. A potential role opens for onboard carbon capture and storage (oCCS). Eastern Pacific Shipping’s Pacific Cobalt became the first classed commercial oCCS installation in 2024 under LR’s Emission Abatement Carbon Capture & Storage (EACCS) (Amine, HFO) class notation, while Solvang’s Clipper Eris is testing a full-scale system designed to capture around 70% of the CO₂ produced by its main engine. For the right vessel types and trades, it offers a realistic pathway to reducing CO₂ emissions and managing carbon costs while fuel supply chains, infrastructure and regulations continue to evolve.” The strongest opportunities for oCCS are likely to be those vessels with sufficient remaining trading life and space for the equipment. The IMO is still developing a global framework covering safety, testing, verification and carbon accounting. Entering an oCCS world oCCS could offer an emissions-reduction pathway for suitable vessels using fossil fuels or their artificial equivalents as the transition to zero and near-zero emission fuels develops. Regulation also needs to recognise the resulting emissions reduction, to help create a working carbon economy.

items.summary: The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of their fuels beginning in 2030. The Department for Transport’s proposal , published Monday, November 16, would establish a fuel standard broadly aligned with the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime regulation while leaving room for adjustments as international negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) continue. Under the government’s preferred approach, the rules would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above, regardless of flag, covering approximately 5,000 vessels based on historical port-call data. The UK Chamber of Shipping welcomed the consultation but urged policymakers to ensure that new requirements reflect the availability of alternative fuels, supporting infrastructure and commercially viable technologies. According to the government’s consultation, approximately 97% of ships above 5,000 gross tonnage that called at UK ports in 2019 also called at EU ports. The proposed fuel regulation would complement the UK’s existing maritime carbon-pricing measures, including the extension of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to domestic shipping in July 2026.

items.summary: LONDON, Nov 16 (Reuters) – The cost of shipping oil in the largest tankers has declined sharply since the beginning of November, reflecting weaker demand for chartering and an unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium that sent shipping costs to a record high in October. Freight ?rates for supertankers, also known as very large crude carriers (VLCCs), carrying ?oil from the Gulf of Oman to China fell to about 308 ?on the Worldscale basis on November 13, down by 64% from their record high of 841 on October 8, Baltic Exchange data shows. The plunge in rates came as Gulf oil exporters increased crude flows towards levels seen before the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Vortexa analyst Ioannis Papadimitriou said the recent spike in freight rates had reduced Asian demand for longer-haul US, West African and North Sea crude, which in turn increased the region’s use of Middle East crude, and that VLCC demand for longer voyages dropped as a result. “As more tonnage is freed up, rates come under downward pressure.” Rates fell even more sharply on other routes, such as from West Africa to Asia. items.summary: Stock image: A Maersk containership is seen near Suez Canal Bridge which is known as the "Peace Bridge" in the Suez Canal, Egypt, August 6, 2023. Suez Canal Authority/Handout via REUTERS Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd are bringing three more Gemini Cooperation services back through the Red Sea and Suez Canal, marking another major step in the container shipping industry’s gradual return to the shorter route between Asia and Europe. The carriers announced Monday that their AE1, AE2 and AE3 services will shift from sailing around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope to transiting the Suez Canal, with the changes taking effect between December 2026 and January 2027. In September, the two carriers announced the rerouting of four additional Gemini services — AE5, AE11, AE12 and ME2 — joining two services already using the canal. Earlier this month, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd also announced the return of their ME1 service connecting India and Europe, with the first revised sailings scheduled for November 4 and 13. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd said they will continue closely monitoring developments in the Middle East, with any further changes to the Gemini network dependent on continued stability in the Red Sea. The announcement underscores the industry’s growing willingness to restore regular Suez Canal operations, while stopping short of suggesting that security risks in the region have disappeared.

items.title: How reliable in predicting spot prices is box ship utilisation?
items.original_title: How reliable in predicting spot prices is box ship utilisation?
items.summary: The relationship between vessel utilisation and container spot freight rates is markedly different on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades. New analysis from Sea-Intelligence raises questions over how reliably capacity utilisation can predict pricing. The analyst found a strong correlation between utilisation and spot rates on the transpacific, where freight rates rise sharply once vessel utilisation exceeds 90%. On the transpacific, the analysis identified a clear relationship between utilisation and freight rates, with the strongest correlation, 71%, occurring when spot rates lagged changes in utilisation by one month. A further analysis of utilisation against spot rates showed freight rates begin climbing steeply once utilisation passes 90%, reflecting a tightening capacity market in which shippers compete for available slots. Its correlation analysis and scatter plot showed changes in nominal vessel utilisation were a poor indicator of spot rate movements on the trade, which the analyst suggested reflected fundamental differences in the structure of the two trades. On the transpacific, most vessel capacity is dedicated to cargo moving between Asia and North America, making utilisation a relatively direct measure of the balance between supply and demand, while Asia-Europe is more complex, as vessels carry cargo for multiple markets through major transhipment hubs along their routes.

items.title: Smaller US truckers buckling under as costs outpace rate gains
items.original_title: Smaller US truckers buckling under as costs outpace rate gains
items.summary: As rising costs outpace rate increases, the pool of truckers in North America continues to shrink – and industry experts see no end to the bloodletting. Industry reports show a steady increase in casualties in the trucking industry: in the five weeks from mid-September into October ,at least 16 carriers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, or simply collapsed with Chapter 7 submissions. Bankruptcy filings have occurred all across the US, many are small and mid-sized truckers, tanging from owner-operators with a single vehicle to firms fielding 50-100 trucks, crushed by liabilities of several hundred thousand dollars up to several million. Recent filings include Silk Route Transportation from Maryland (12 trucks in its fleet), buckling under liabilities of $541,000, and California-based Road King Transport (20 trucks), with almost $3.4m in debts. Elevated fuel costs have been a heavy burden, which has fallen disproportionately on smaller outfits that do not have fuel surcharge mechanisms to mitigate the impact, as the pricing over load boards is all-inclusive. According to Satish Jindel, founder and president of SJ Consulting, the hit from fuel cost is not as heavy as the rise in insurance costs in the wake of the Montgomery lawsuit ruling of May, which found brokers and 3PLs liable in cases of serious crashes involving truckers they hire.

With Brussels preparing to ban Russian LNG imports from January 1, 2027, European buyers continue to provide Moscow with a lucrative market, despite repeated political commitments to end the bloc’s dependence on Russian energy following the invasion of Ukraine. Urgewald analysed data from energy intelligence firm Kpler showing that EU ports received 12.89 million tonnes of LNG from Russia’s Yamal project between January and October, up 6.3% year-on-year and accounting for 81% of the project’s recorded deliveries worldwide. Europe remains the main customer of one of Russia’s flagship Arctic gas projects, the Yamal pipeline, despite EU leaders repeatedly touting the end of reliance on Russian fossil fuels. With just 50 days until the ban on Russian LNG imports under existing long-term contracts takes effect, EU purchases continue to rise. Spain (2.91 million tonnes), the Netherlands (1.32 million tonnes) and Portugal (0.22 million tonnes) were also among the Russian Arctic LNG recipients in October. “We can end Russian LNG imports on 1 January.

items.title: Copper Sinks to Near Five-Month Low
items.original_title: Copper Sinks to Near Five-Month Low
items.summary: Copper futures declined to around $6.00 per pound on Monday, reaching their lowest levels since June as concerns surrounding the artificial intelligence sector and a strengthening US dollar weighed on the metal. AI-related stocks faced renewed selling pressure ahead of Nvidia’s earnings report and Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO this week, dampening market sentiment toward copper. The metal is closely linked to the global AI expansion due to its importance in data centers and power infrastructure. Additional pressure came from a rising US dollar as expectations of more aggressive Federal Reserve rate hikes continued to grow. A stronger dollar makes dollar-denominated commodities such as copper more expensive for buyers using other currencies. Meanwhile, increasing inventories on the London Metal Exchange added to the downward pressure, with stockpiles reaching approximately 320,000 tons by mid-November, significantly higher than the August low of 205,000 tons. Source: Trading Economics
